html:
The map's label for coastal peoples of South America who lived mainly on shellfish and fish, shown from 1500 BCE to 800 CE. The best known are the builders of the sambaquis, great shell mounds along the Atlantic coast of southern Brazil, and the label most likely marks them.

The sambaquis are heaps of shells, sand, bones and ash, some more than 30 m high, built up over centuries. They were also cemeteries: people buried their dead in them, with offerings. Their makers carved fine stone and bone figures of fish and birds. Studies of their bones suggest fish, more than shellfish, was their main food.

Shell mounds were built on this coast for thousands of years. In the first millennium CE building slowed as pottery-making peoples from the interior moved toward the coast. Later Tupi farmers took over much of the shore, and they were the people the Portuguese met when they founded Portuguese Brazil. Other shellfish-based ways of life lasted far to the south among the Patagonian canoe peoples.
